This study guide has been compiled by hand from all 13 course files of «Introduction to Engineering» (code
CC-INEN010104, 4 ECTS, fall semester 2026/27, Tashkent University of Technology, Faculty of Power
Engineering). It covers the material of the first four weeks: every savol (savollar — questions), topshiriq

and supplied with a model answer. The guide is built so that you can prepare for the weekly mini projects
(30%), the midterm (30%) and the final (40%) without going back through hundreds of slides and pages.
The course is taught by Dr. Mohammad Reza Bahrami (lectures; Dean of the Faculty of Power Engineering,
PhD in Mechanical Engineering, professor at Innopolis University, adjunct professor at Constructor
University Bremen) and Ibrokhimjon Khamidov (labs; assistant professor, MSc/PhD track at Politecnico di
Milano, research — lean manufacturing, sustainability, quantitative productivity assessment). The course
follows the Project-Based Learning approach: all semester work revolves around one team system, which
each team chooses in week 2 and carries through to the final report.

1.1. How the course and the grading system work
From the syllabus: the workload is 120 hours (4 ECTS × 30 h) — 30 hours of lectures, 30 hours of in-class
team project work, 60 hours of independent study. There are no prerequisites, and the course is open to all
first-year students; what is expected is working with basic quantitative logic, active participation in
teamwork, and clear oral and written communication in English. The five intended learning outcomes
(ILOs), with their Bloom's taxonomy levels and mapping to the ASIIN competencies:
• ILO-1 (Understand, subject competency) — explain that engineering models are purposeful
simplifications of complex systems, and describe how assumptions and approximations shape a model's
usefulness and limitations.
• ILO-2 (Apply, subject competency) — apply basic quantitative reasoning (demand and capacity, rates
and flows, order-of-magnitude estimates) to characterize the behavior of a real system from incomplete
data.
• ILO-3 (Analyze, methodological competency) — analyze system dynamics (delays, queues, capacity,
bottlenecks) and use simple simulations under uncertainty.
• ILO-4 (Evaluate, systemic competency) — evaluate trade-offs between competing objectives
(efficiency, cost, fairness, accessibility) and justify a design decision taking technical, ethical and
stakeholder considerations into account.
• ILO-5 (Apply, social competency) — collaborate effectively in a team throughout the semester project
and present models, assumptions and decisions clearly in writing and orally.

2. Week 1 — Engineering as a Profession
2.1. Key points (the «all qoidalar (rules)» of Week 1)
Etymology and definition. The word «engineer» comes from the Latin ingenium — «the fruit of genius, a
talented invention» — and the verb ingeniare — «to devise, to invent». About 2,000 years ago ingenium
described the designing of a new machine; the word then shifted to the machines themselves, and later to the
people who designed them — the «engine-ers». The same root survives today in the French/German
ingénieur and the Italian ingegnere. Course definition: an engineer is «a creative, inventive person who finds
solutions to practical problems». The modern definition of engineering: engineering is the practice of using
natural science, mathematics and the engineering design process to solve technical problems, to raise
efficiency and productivity, and to improve systems. Kosky (ch. 1) adds: engineers use creative design and
analysis — involving energy, materials, motion and information — to serve human needs, and they express
their knowledge in the form of variables, numbers and units.
«Science can amuse and fascinate us all, but it is engineering that changes the world» — Isaac
Asimov.
«Scientists investigate that which already is; engineers create that which has never been» —
Albert Einstein.
Fields of engineering. The classical fields from the lecture: civil (roads, bridges, water systems), mechanical
(machines, engines, robots), electrical (power, circuits, control), computer (hardware and software),
chemical (processes, materials, fuels), aerospace (aircraft and spacecraft), biomedical (medical devices),
environmental (water, air, sustainable development); plus agricultural, ceramic, industrial, manufacturing,
marine, materials, mining, nuclear, petroleum, textile and others. A historical note from Kosky: the oldest
kind of engineering is military (fortifications, siege works, roads for armies); the first non-military engineers

were called civilian engineers, which was shortened to civil engineers; civil engineering is one of the oldest
continuously practiced disciplines.
Fig. 1. Classical fields of engineering (week 1): the eight disciplines from the lecture and their focus.
A common misconception (NOT THE SAME AS). Engineering is not repair. A plumber installs and fixes
pipes — an engineer designs the water supply system: pipe diameters, pressures and layouts are chosen
before anything is built. A car mechanic repairs a vehicle — an engineer designs its parts: the engine, the
transmission and the safety systems that the mechanic later services. This distinction is a favorite
comprehension-check question: engineering = design and analysis before, and instead of, repair.
Historical role. The four eras from the lecture: the Industrial Revolution (steam, railways, factory
production), electrification (electric power and telecommunications connecting cities and industries), the age
of aviation and the automobile (flight and mass mobility, compressing distance and time), and the digital and
information age (computing, the internet, software). In each era it was engineers who turned new scientific
knowledge into the tools, systems and infrastructure that people actually use. A quote from James Kip Finch:
«The engineer has been, and is, a maker of history».
Social role. Engineers shape the everyday conditions of life: the water we drink, the energy in our homes,
hospitals, roads. Engineers sit «at the interface between science and society» (Gordon Stanley Brown, MIT):
they translate scientific possibilities into products, systems and infrastructure that reach millions of people,
so their decisions carry direct social consequences — safety, health, fairness, the environment. That is
exactly why engineering is organized as a profession, with codes of ethics and standards of practice. The
mission of the century was formulated by the US National Academy of Engineering (NAE Grand
Challenges — 14 in total, 6 are given in the lecture): provide access to clean water; restore and improve
urban infrastructure; advance health informatics; make solar energy economical; secure cyberspace; engineer

better medicines (the full list also covers energy, the brain, learning and scientific discovery).
Economic role (the lecture's numbers): more than 1.6 million engineers work in the United States alone;
engineering is the country's second-largest profession; the average starting salary of an engineering graduate
in the US is $68,000 a year (2017 data from NACE, repeated in Kosky ch. 1). An engineering degree is a
springboard: graduates routinely move into medicine, law, business and public service. Beyond careers,
engineering is an engine of national development: this is how countries build the infrastructure, industry and
technological base on which economic growth depends. Moaveni (ch. 1, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics
data) gives the employment distribution: 1,572,100 engineers in total, of them civil — 278,400 (17.7%),
mechanical — 238,700 (15.2%), industrial — 214,800 (13.7%), electrical — 157,800 (10.0%); most
engineering degrees are awarded in the electrical, mechanical and civil specializations — the «parents of all
the other branches».
Culture, identity and professional societies. The word «engineer» is strikingly uniform across languages — a
reflection of a shared identity that crosses borders. Engineers usually work in teams — from two or three
people to hundreds on a single large project (for example, the design of a passenger aircraft). Professional
societies reinforce that shared identity: they define the standards, continuing education and ethics of each
discipline. The key societies of the lecture: ASME — mechanical; IEEE — electrical/computers; ASCE —
civil; AIChE — chemical; AIAA — aerospace; ANS — nuclear. Kosky adds ASTM (materials and testing)
and BMES (biomedical). A typical engineering society (a Kosky footnote) defines the disciplines required
for membership, advocates for them, sets codes and standards, provides additional educational courses and
maintains its own code of ethics.
The ten traits of the «problem-solver DNA» (mindset of a good problem solver) — the shared list of the
lecture and Lab 1: objective, analytical, creative, dedicated, curious, courageous, adventurous, enthusiastic,
patient, vigilant. In the lab, each person chooses their trait, and groups are formed so that the mix of traits is
diverse: «a group of five Objective members will argue with itself forever and never solve anything».
Moaveni (ch. 1) gives a parallel list of the common traits of good engineers: engineers are problem solvers;
they have a firm command of fundamental principles; they are analytical, attentive to detail and creative;
they want to learn throughout their lives; they carry a portable core of knowledge (a good mechanical
engineer can work as an automotive, aerospace or chemical engineer); they have written and oral
communication skills; they manage their time; they have «people skills»; they write reports; they use
computers freely for modeling; they participate actively in professional organizations; they work in a team
environment.
Science — engineering — design (the week's triad). Science investigates what already exists, asks «why does
this happen?» and looks for explanations, generalizable laws and truth about the natural world. Engineering
creates what has never existed, asks «how do we make it work?» and applies scientific knowledge under real
constraints to build a solution. Design is the creative, open-ended act of giving a solution its form: shape,
aesthetics and user experience; engineering design is design disciplined by analysis: physics, materials, cost,
manufacturability and safety constrain the possibilities. The «bridge test»: if a bridge is given a striking
shape with no regard for load-bearing capacity, that is design without engineering; if the shape is derived
from an analysis of loads, materials and structural integrity, that is engineering design. Steve Jobs's quote
from the lecture: «Design is not how it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works». The connection

2.2. Week-1 ethics qoidalar (rules): the NSPE codes and personal ethics
Ethics is the central theme of week 1 (the lecture + all of Lab 1 + Kosky ch. 1 + Moaveni ch. 5). A
professional code of ethics aims to ensure that the profession serves the legitimate purposes of all
stakeholders: oneself, the employer, the profession and society. The code protects the members of the
profession from the unwanted consequences of competition (the pressure to «cut corners» for the sake of
savings), while leaving them free to enjoy its desirable consequences — invention and innovation. Armed
with the code, an engineer can resist the pressure with the phrase: «As a professional, I cannot ethically place
business interests above professional ethics».
The fundamental canons of the NSPE (National Society of Professional Engineers), the full version from
Kosky 1.10.2 — engineers, in the fulfillment of their professional duties, shall:
1. Hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public.
2. Perform services only in areas of their competence.
3. Issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner.
4. Act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees.
5. Avoid deceptive acts.
6. Conduct themselves honorably, responsibly, ethically, and lawfully so as to enhance the honor,
reputation, and usefulness of the profession.

Fig. 2. Engineering ethics (week 1): the six NSPE fundamental canons and the five cornerstones of personal ethics.
The Lab 1 adaptation of the ten canons (the handout «The 10 Canons of the Code», NSPE adapted) — the
formulations are shorter, and these are the convenient ones to memorize: 1) Safety first — the safety, health
and welfare of the public comes before everything; 2) Stay in your lane — work only within your area of
competence; 3) Speak truthfully — public statements only objective and truthful; 4) No conflicts of
interest — be a faithful agent, do not allow personal interest to conflict with duty; 5) No deception — avoid
all deceptive acts; 6) Act honorably — behave responsibly, protecting the reputation of the profession; 7) No
hidden payments — do not take payment from more than one interested party without full consent; 8) Don't
misrepresent yourself — never falsify your qualifications, experience or results; 9) Give proper credit —
acknowledge the real contribution of others; 10) Don't stay silent — report, or refuse to approve, violations
of the norms, even under pressure.
The five cornerstones of personal ethical behavior (Five Cornerstones, Kosky 1.9.1): 1) do what you say you
will do; 2) never disclose information given to you in confidence; 3) take responsibility for your actions (and
mistakes); 4) never participate in a lie; 5) never accept gifts that would compromise your ability to act in the
best interests of your organization. Kosky notes that the list is incomplete: it lacks the «golden rule» common
to most ethical codes of the world («Do not do to others what you do not wish for yourself» — Confucius's
version).
The top-10 questions to ask yourself when making a personal ethical decision (Kosky 1.9.2, counting from
the 10th to the 1st): 10) Could the decision become a habit? If yes — don't do it. 9) Is it legal? If not — don't
do it. 8) Is it safe? If not — don't do it. 7) Is it right? If not — don't do it. 6) Would it withstand public
scrutiny? If not — don't do it. 5) If something terrible happens, will I be able to defend my actions? If not —

don't do it. 4) Is it fair, balanced and honest? If not — don't do it. 3) How will it make me feel about myself?
If terrible — don't do it. 2) Does this choice lead to the greatest good for the greatest number of people? If
not — don't do it. 1) And question No. 1: would I do this in front of my mother? If not — don't do it.
The Engineering Ethics Decision Matrix (Kosky 1.11) — the course's main tool. The rows of the matrix are
the NSPE canons; the columns are possible courses of action (for example: go along with the decision; appeal
to upper management; resign; write to your congressman; call a journalist). Each cell receives a brief answer
to the question «does this particular course of action satisfy this particular canon?» (yes/no/maybe, with a
note). Then the «yes» and «no» answers are summed across each column (ignoring the «maybes») — the
criterion suggests the first action. The value of the matrix: it is «divide and conquer» — it forces you to
consider all the dimensions instead of the first yes/no that comes to mind, and it prompts you to list all the
relevant considerations. The exception: if one criterion overrides all the others — follow it.
The Engineer's Creed (NSPE 1954, from Moaveni ch. 5): «To give the utmost of performance; to participate
in none but honest enterprise; to live and work according to the laws of man and the highest standards of
professional conduct; to place service before profit, the honor and standing of the profession before personal
advantage, and the public welfare above all other considerations». Moaveni also defines the terms: academic
dishonesty (cheating, plagiarism, marking attendance for another person), plagiarism (presenting someone
else's work as your own without citation), conflict of interest (a clash between personal interests and the
duties of a position), contract (a voluntary agreement of two or more parties; legally binding), professional
responsibility (the responsibility connected with possessing specialized knowledge and using it for the
benefit of society).

Q: Lecture, interactive 1: «Why do you want to become an engineer?» (an answer in one or two words,
not graded).
Answer: The model answer is built on three typical motives that the lecture itself suggests for reflection: (1)
an inspiring person (a teacher, an engineer parent, a famous engineer); (2) a problem you wanted to solve
(for example, power cuts made you want to understand power systems); (3) a favorite school subject
(mathematics, physics). A strong answer ties the personal motive to the definition of engineering: «I want to
be one of the people who turn scientific knowledge into working solutions».
Q: Lecture, interactive 2: «Which field of engineering interests you the most?» — why did you choose
exactly this one?
Answer: Any answer is correct — this is an introduction to the audience. A model justification: name the
field (for example, energy/electrical), connect it to specific products from the lecture's list (power, circuits,
control systems) and to the NAE Grand Challenge it addresses (for example, «make solar energy
economical»), and mention the professional society (IEEE).

Q: Lecture, discuss: «Name one ancient or historical structure that you consider a great engineering
achievement. What problem did it solve?»
Answer: Model answer: the pyramids of Giza — the problem of the mass lifting and precise placement of

3.1. Key points (“all qoidalar” of week 2)
A recap of week 1 in one breath (the slides themselves open this way): engineering is a creative, inventive
response to practical problems, not repair work; it has a history — from ancient walls and aqueducts to
steam, electricity, flight, and software; a social role — engineers sit at the interface between science and
society; an economic role — one of the world's largest and best-paid professions; and a common culture —
professional societies, shared traits, and a code of ethics.
Definition of a system (the key definition of the week): a system is a set of interacting elements and
processes that transform inputs into outputs and exists within an operating context. The four parts of the
definition: elements (the parts and the people that make up the system), processes (how the parts interact
and transform things over time), inputs and outputs (what flows in and what flows out), and the operating
context (the conditions under which the system exists).
A system is NOT a pile of parts (NOT THE SAME AS). A random heap of parts is not a system; a system is
parts with a purpose, connected so that they act together rather than simply lie together. Four “not a system /
system” pairs from the lecture: a pile of bricks in the yard — a brick wall (bricks + mortar + a load path,
holding the weight together); a student, a timetable, and a bus stop taken separately — a university bus route
(vehicles, schedule, and passengers interact to move people); a stove, a refrigerator, and a sink standing in a
room — a cafeteria kitchen (staff, equipment, and a workflow that turns ingredients into meals); a phone, a

The system boundary. The boundary is a drawn line, often imaginary, separating “inside the system” from
“outside”. Anything may cross it: materials, people, money, information, energy. The key idea of the week:
the boundary is an engineer's choice, not a fact about the world. You can draw it tightly around one
machine or broadly around an entire building — each choice changes what has to be analyzed. Lab 2 repeats
the same rule: “the boundary is drawn, not discovered”; two engineers may draw the boundary of the same
system in different places — both choices are valid, provided the choice is justified and applied consistently.
The operating context. Just outside the boundary sits the operating context — conditions that do not cross the
boundary as inputs yet still constrain the system's behavior. The four categories from the lecture: codes and
standards (sanitary, safety, building); time and schedule (opening hours, the academic calendar, deadlines);
existing infrastructure (what is already built and with which the system must coexist); budget and resources
(what funding, staffing, and materials are actually available). The cafeteria example worked through:
inputs — food deliveries, staff arriving, students coming in; outputs — meals served, food waste, payments;
context — the sanitary code, opening hours, the kitchen budget, the building layout.
Stakeholders. A stakeholder is anyone who uses the system, runs it, or is affected by it — whether or not they
sit inside the boundary. The three columns of the stakeholder map: Uses It — uses it (students eating in the
cafeteria; bus passengers); Runs It — runs it (kitchen staff, dispatchers, maintenance crews); Affected By
It — affected by it (neighbors living with the noise, the trucks, the congestion — often entirely outside the
boundary). The stakeholder map is a simple table; “a first draft is enough to get started”. Importantly,
stakeholders do not always want the same thing. Good systems thinking notices the tension instead of hiding
it. The lecture example: the university wants the bus route to be faster; the maintenance crew — safer; the
passengers — cheaper. Question: who are the stakeholders here, and where is the tension?

4.1. Key points (“all qoidalar” of week 3)
A recap of week 2 (in one breath): a system is interacting elements and processes turning inputs into outputs;
the boundary is a line the engineer chooses; the operating context constrains the system from just outside the
boundary; stakeholders are those who use it, run it, or are affected by it. Today — what happens inside the

What a PFD is: a process flow diagram shows the steps of a process in order and what flows between them.
Three things it gives you: the sequence (what happens first, next, and last); the flow (what moves between
the steps: material, people, information, money, energy); the problems (gaps, waits, loops, and hand-offs
become visible). Kosky et al. apply the same idea to the design process itself (Fig. 21.1): the design process
is a process too.
Elements are nouns, processes are verbs. The cafeteria's elements: cooks, ovens, trays, tables, students. The

One process — three levels of detail (rule: choose the level to fit the question, and keep one level per
diagram). Level 0 (black box): inputs come in, outputs go out, the inside is hidden — the cafeteria: food,
staff, and students come in; meals, waste, and payments go out. Level 1 (main steps): a handful of main steps
inside the boundary — Receive deliveries → Store ingredients → Prepare meals → Serve meals → Take
payment → Clear and dispose. Level 2 (zoom in): one level-1 step expanded into its own diagram —
“Prepare meals”: wash → chop → cook → hold hot.
The five symbols of the PFD language (course convention): Start/End — where the process begins and ends;
Step — a single action, named “verb + noun”; Decision — a question with labeled Yes/No exits; Flow — an
arrow for the order of the steps and for what moves; Wait/queue — where things sit and wait (course
convention — a dashed box). “Five symbols are enough for the course; the sequence matters more than the
particular choice of symbols”.
Five rules for a readable diagram (memorize them): 1) Start and end explicitly: one start, and every path
reaches an end. 2) Name the steps “verb + noun”: “Receive deliveries”, not “Delivery”. 3) Label the arrows:
say what moves — food, students, information, money. 4) Give every decision both exits: every Yes and
every No must lead somewhere. 5) Keep one level of detail: arrows crossing the boundary are your inputs
and outputs.
Every arrow carries something (five categories — the same as for the week-2 inputs and outputs): material
(ingredients, trays, food waste), people (students in a queue), information (menus, orders, meal-plan
verification), money (payments, supplier bills), energy (gas, electricity, hot water). Label every arrow with
what moves: it shows what the next step needs.

start/end symbols → add Start and End; error 2 — “Kitchen” is a place, not a step → rename it “Prepare
meals”; error 3 — the decision has only a “Yes” exit → add a “No” exit, e.g. “Prepare more meals”; error 4 —
“Chop onions” is level-2 detail → keep one level: “Prepare meals”; error 5 — unlabeled arrows → label what
moves: students, meals, money. The rules matter because the reader should never have to guess.

A diagram is a model with a purpose (Harry Beck's example, the London Underground map of the early
1930s): it gives up real distances and street geography, but keeps the stations, the lines, and the interchanges.
What it keeps: stations · lines · connections and interchanges; what it drops: real distances · street layout ·

One system — five perspectives (the bus route through five pairs of eyes): Rider — Walk to the stop → Wait

Maintenance crew — Inspect → Diagnose → Repair → Return to service; success = safe buses, planned

success = cost per passenger, coverage, few complaints. Neighbor — Hear the bus → Notice the traffic →

picture starts at the stop, the driver's — at the depot), different steps (each includes what they see), different
definitions of success (faster/safer/cheaper turn into competing definitions of a good job). “No single
diagram is wrong. Each is a model built with a purpose. Good engineers draw several and ask: whose view is

How pollution is measured (18.3): the amount of a pollutant is given by its concentration — mass per unit
volume of the mixture. Formula (18.1): CA = mA/Vmixture = mA/(VA + VB + VC). For water: 1 ppm = 1
mg/L and 1 ppb = 1 μg/L; “one cup of pollutant in a swimming pool is ppm, one drop in a swimming pool is
ppb”; 1 g/m3 = 1 mg/L = 1 ppm; 1 mg/m3 = 1 μg/L = 1 ppb. For soil: 1 ppm = 1 mg/kg, 1 ppb = 1 μg/kg. For
air: concentrations in mg/m3 depend on temperature and pressure, so they are standardized at 1 atm (101,325
N/m2) and 25 °C (298 K); the molar volume Vmolar = RT/p = 8.3143 × 298/101325 = 0.02445 m3/mol =
24.45 L/mol. Conversion (18.2a): concentration (mg/m3) = concentration (ppm) × M/(24.45 L/mol); (18.2b):
concentration (ppm) = concentration (mg/m3) × 24.45/M, where M is the molar mass of the gas. Example
18.1: CO2 at 405 ppm in 2017 → 405 × 44/24.45 = 729 mg/m3.
The mass balance equation (18.3a) — the main tool: [mass accumulated in the control volume] = [total mass
that entered] − [total mass that left] + [mass created or destroyed inside]. The rate form (18.3b): (ṁ)CV =
Σ(ṁ)in − Σ(ṁ)out + Ṁ G, where ṁ = dm/dt is the mass flow rate, and Ṁ G is the generation rate inside the
control volume due to reactions. Mass as such is neither created nor destroyed (except in nuclear reactions),
but the mass of particular chemical species can be created/destroyed by reactions (2H2 + O2 → 2H2O).
Example 18.2 (cited by lecture 3): the Transfer Center receives 600.0 tons/day of solid waste from one
community and 400.0 tons/day from another; 25% of the total is recyclables; the incinerator at full capacity
burns 200.0 tons/day. How much waste should be planned for landfill disposal? Need — the rate of disposal
to the landfill; Know — the mass flow rates at the input and output; How — define the system as the
Transfer Center, draw a control volume with the inflows and outflows, apply the balance (18.3b); Solve:
there are no reactions, so Ṁ G = 0, and there is no accumulation, so (ṁ)CV = 0 = Σ(ṁ)in − Σ(ṁ)out; 0 = (600
+ 400) − [0.250 × (600 + 400) + 200 + ṁLF]; ṁLF = 550.0 tons/day.
Linking concentration and flow rate (18.4): ṁp = CpQf, where Qf = dV/dt is the volumetric flow rate of the
carrier medium (m3/s), and Cp is the concentration of the pollutant. An alternative form of the balance
(18.5): (ṁp)CV = 0 = Σ(CpQf)in − Σ(CpQf)out + Ṁ Gp. If the pollutant's volume is small relative to the
water/air, the equation C = 1.0 (100%) is added at the inputs and outputs for the carrier medium. Example
18.3: a factory emits 50.0 kg/day of SO2; a wind of 6.00 m/s drives 7.00×106 m3/s of air with a background

Four kinds of information (the Kosky ch. 23 classification, “Clarifying the Problem”): Fact — something

personal view or preference (“the cafeteria should open a second serving line”). All four are useful: opinions
and guesses show what people care about; facts tell you what is happening. But only facts and good
inferences may anchor a problem statement.
The three-step check of what you hear (Test What You Hear): 1) Hear — collect what people say, including
opinions and guesses; 2) Observe and measure — watch the process; count, time, ask stakeholders directly;
3) Decide — keep what the facts support; reframe what they contradict. Example: many shoppers say the
store needs more cash registers; watching the queue all day and talking with the manager may confirm this —
or reveal a different cause. Your Week 3 PFD tells you where to look: at the steps, the waits and the
hand-offs.

and a method.

An engineering variable: a variable is a quantity that can be measured, expressed as a number with units.
Time is measured with a clock (seconds, minutes), length with a ruler (metres), temperature with a
thermometer (°C or kelvins), counts with “how many students, meals, buses”. Speed, for example, combines
a ruler measurement (distance) with a clock measurement (time). A number without units is incomplete:
“Waiting time: 12” — 12 seconds? 12 minutes? A student at the front of the queue and a student at the back
would read it very differently; “Speed limit: 100” — 100 km/h ≈ 62 mph: one number, two different speeds.
In engineering a result has two parts — the value and the units — and both must be right (Kosky ch. 2).
Variables live on the diagram: every step and arrow of the Week 3 PFD suggests what can be counted, timed
or weighed. Cafeteria: 1 Receive deliveries — deliveries per day (count/day); 2 Prepare meals — meals
prepared per hour; 3 Serve meals — waiting time at the line (min); 4 Take payment — payments per minute
(count/min); 5 Clear and dispose — food waste (kg/day).

hour; waste, kg/day); design variables — what we can change (the number of serving lines, staff per shift,
menu size); context variables — what we cannot change (opening hours, sanitation codes, building size).

the limits.

many?” or “how much?”. “If you cannot picture how to measure it — keep looking.”

alongside style is engineering design. Until the 1960s this description was sufficient; today the definition has

engineering approach minimises the number of design iterations — fewer iterations = cheaper and faster.
Design problems versus homework problems: a homework problem has a single unique answer, found by a
logical method (need-know-how-solve); a design problem has no unique answer — several designs may
satisfy the statement; there may be a “best” answer with respect to the critical requirements (a design that
minimises unit cost may be unreliable — if reliability is critical to the client, it is not the “best” answer). The
qualities of a good designer (Kosky 21.5): curiosity about how things work (take devices apart — reverse
engineering; stroll through a toy store); selflessness (suppress your ego for the sake of the team); fearlessness
(step into the unknown); persistence (failures are inevitable); adaptability (“if the ship is sinking, don't go
down with it — redesign it”).
The design notebook (design notebook, 21.6) and the Gordon Gould case: a permanently bound notebook
with numbered pages; on the night of November 9, 1957, Columbia University graduate student Gould wrote
down and sketched the idea of amplifying light — “light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation”
(laser) — and on the Wednesday had the notes notarised by a notary in a candy store; for 30 years he litigated
patents against rivals whose filings came later, and won millions in royalties thanks to a notarised, clear and
contemporaneous record. Rules for keeping the notebook: date and number every page; do not tear out
pages; do not leave blank pages (cross them out with a diagonal); enter all data, descriptions, sketches,
calculations; an index on the first page; write in real time, without rewriting a fair copy; write in pen; do not
use correction fluid — strike through; paste in computer printouts, graphs, photographs; write as if someone
else will read it; document the team meetings (date, results, tasks).
The eight steps of the engineering design process (Kosky 21.8, Fig. 21.1 — also a PFD!): 1) Define the
problem. 2) Generate alternative concepts. 3) Evaluate and select a concept. 4) Detail the design. 5) Defend
the design (design defense). 6) Manufacture and test. 7) Evaluate the performance. 8) Prepare the final

and information gathering done before the final design is fixed. The “Tower” exercise: the tallest tower out

Dym, chapter 1 “Engineering Design” — the vocabulary of design. Three roles in any project: the client
(client — the one who wants the design to be conceived), the user (user — the one who will use it), the
designer (designer). Dym's formal definition: engineering design is a systematic, intellectual process in
which engineers generate, evaluate and specify solutions for devices, systems or processes whose
forms and functions achieve the clients' objectives and the users' needs while satisfying the specified
constraints. The vocabulary: a design objective (design objective) — a property or behaviour we want; a
constraint (constraint) — a limit/bound on properties or behaviour; violating it makes the design
unacceptable (binary: yes/no, no intermediate states); a function (function) — what the device must do;
engineering functions almost always involve the transformation or transmission of energy, information or
material; a means (means) — a way to accomplish a function (friction is a means of braking force); form
(form) — shape and structure as opposed to material. Objectives may be met fully, partially or not met;
constraints must always be satisfied — hence the difference between “as cheap as possible” (an objective)
and “cheaper than $20” (a constraint).
Metrics and specifications (Dym 1.2.3): a metric (metric) — the scale on which achievement of an objective
is measured; a specification (specification) — the scale on which the performance of functions is measured;
the terms requirements and specifications are often synonymous, but Dym separates them: requirements —
the client's requirements (objectives, constraints and functions in the client's words), specifications —
engineering specifications (the designer's expression in engineering terms). Form and function are
independent: from a smartphone's form you cannot infer its purpose, and knowing the function “wireless
telephony” does not suggest the form. All design is systematic design (Herbert Simon: “design is the activity

interface between the inner and outer environments”); the future challenges — complex systems (the
interstate highways, the power grid, the internet). Communication: the product of design is usually a set of

(Kansas City, 1981): the contractor could not obtain 24-foot threaded rods and hung the second-floor

load; 114 people died and the losses ran into millions; the lesson — the specifications must be complete and
unambiguous, conveying the designer's intent; design is a human, social activity.

“why?” questions move up (“a useful ladder” → “a marketable one”), “how?” questions move down; when the

all objectives are measured consistently so that none dominates by its scale; if the measurement is too

Dym, chapter 5 “Identifying Constraints”: a constraint is a limit or a prohibition on properties/behaviour;
usually a binary choice (the material is a conductor or not; the deflection of a step is less than 0.05 inches or

exploring what remains; a constraint is “weeding out”, an objective is “choosing among the acceptable”.

“satisfice”; one can minimally satisfy OSHA or significantly exceed it (a “super-safe ladder”) for the sake of
marketing. Example: the objective “an inexpensive ladder” + the constraint “no more than $25” — first the
weeding-out by the constraint, then the choice by the price and the other objectives. The constraints for the

Dym, chapter 6 “Establishing Functions”: a function is what the device must do; a systems view helps — to
do something = to transform an input into an output (y = f(x)). A bookcase “does nothing, it just stands
there” — that is untrue: it resists the force of gravity in order to hold the books, and it allows organising them
on shelves. Misunderstanding all the functions can be tragic (Hyatt Regency). The tools for establishing the
functions: 1) Black box → glass box: draw the system with the inputs on the left and the outputs on the right
(a drill: inputs — electrical power, a supporting force, speed/direction control; output — a rotating chuck),
then “lift the lid” and expose the subfunctions (the cord transmits the energy → the switch directs and
transmits information → the universal motor turns electricity into mechanics → the transmission steps up the
torque, reducing the rotor's 30,000 rpm to the chuck's 2500 rpm); reflect the physics: “to tune a radio” = to
select a frequency in the RF spectrum, not “to turn the knob”; boundaries drawn too wide — you include
functions beyond your control; too narrow — you constrain the design (is a radio's output the electrical signal
to the speakers or the sound from the speakers?). 2) Dissection / reverse engineering: take the device apart
and ask what function each part performs (an exploded view of the DeWalt drill: cord, switch, motor,
transmission — the same functional map as the glass box). 3) Enumeration: list all the functions; the trick is
“what if X disappeared?” (without the bridge, the cars fall into the river → the function is to carry the load;
without the piers, the deck itself would fall → hold up its own weight; the Quebec Bridge collapsed twice, in

7.1. Process and diagram rules
1. The five rules of a readable PFD: one start; every path reaches an end; steps are “verb + noun”; labels
on all arrows; at every decision both outputs (Yes and No) lead somewhere; one level of detail per
diagram.
2. The five PFD symbols of the course: Start/End, Step, Decision, Flow, Wait/queue (dashed frame).
Sequence matters more than the set of symbols.
3. Three levels of detail: Level 0 black box (inputs/outputs), Level 1 main steps, Level 2 zoom in;
choose the level to fit the question.
4. Every arrow carries one of the five flow categories: materials, people, information, money, energy.
5. The system boundary is drawn, not discovered: declare it, justify it, and keep it consistent; arrows
crossing the boundary = inputs and outputs.
6. A system is not a heap of parts: the parts must interact purposefully, transforming inputs into outputs.

7.2. Problem statement and variable rules
1. The solution-free test: a problem statement must not name a device, an application, a vehicle, or a
building; otherwise rewrite it.
2. Statement template: [Stakeholder] needs [outcome] in [system], judged by [measure], within
[constraints].
3. The path: complaint (symptom) → need (what is required) → problem statement (what we are
solving).
4. Sort what you hear: fact / inference / speculation / opinion; only facts and good inferences may
anchor the statement; verify what you hear: hear → observe and measure → decide.
5. A variable = a number + units; if you cannot picture a measurement, keep searching; a useful variable
answers “how much?/how many?”.
6. Three kinds of variables: performance (we are judged on it), design (the levers), context (the limits);
at each PFD step — one variable with its unit.
7. Specifications: each one is a D (demand) or a W (wish); do not turn a wish into a demand; numbers
wherever possible, even rough ones; specifications are independent of the solution.
8. A good performance measure: measurable, relevant, solution-free, concrete (units + target); beware
of averages that hide long tails.
9. Working definition of performance: [system] is judged by [variables with units and targets], through
the eyes of [stakeholders]; write it down and keep the team consistent on it.
10. Need-Know-How-Solve: write Need first; Know — what is known; How — the method and the
assumptions before computing; Solve — compute, check the units, interpret.
7.3. Rules of units, significant figures, and calculations
1. An engineering calculation is right in four ways: variables, number, units, significant figures.
2. Units in calculations: [in], [ft], [in/ft] — brackets on every quantity and factor; units cancel like
fractions.
3. Unit names are lowercase (newton); abbreviations derived from names are capitalized (N); no plurals
(kg, not kgs); no period; two letters only to distinguish units (Wb vs W) and for prefixes (kW).
4. Significant-figure rules: sum/difference — by the decimal positions of the least precise number;
product/quotient — by the number of significant figures of the least precise; rounding 0–4 down, 5–9
up; do not round intermediates.
5. Check unit consistency across the whole system (the Mars Climate Orbiter lesson: pounds-force
versus newtons cost the spacecraft).
6. Order-of-magnitude estimates (Fermi problems): honest rough assumptions → a corridor for the
answer; a check within ~10% is already a success (21 vs 23 barbershops).

7.4. Ethical rules
1. The six NSPE canons: the safety/health/welfare of the public is paramount; practice only within your
area of competence; public statements are objective and truthful; be a faithful agent or trustee; no
deception; act honorably and lawfully — for the honor of the profession.
2. The extended ten (Lab 1): + no hidden payments from several parties; do not misrepresent
qualifications/experience/results; give co-authors due credit; do not stay silent about violations of
standards even under pressure.
3. The five cornerstones of personal ethics: do what you promised; do not disclose what was entrusted to
you; accept responsibility; do not take part in lies; do not accept compromising gifts. (+ the “golden
rule” as a supplement.)
4. The top question of an ethical decision: “Would I do this in front of my mother?” (the full list of
10 — in section 2.2).
5. The ethical decision matrix: rows — the canons, columns — courses of action; “yes/no/maybe” with a
justification; sum the yes/no (ignore the maybes); one overriding criterion cancels the count.
6. TUT course rules: attendance ≥ 75% to be admitted to the final; plagiarism: 1st offense — 0 and a
possible resit, 2nd — 0 without a resit, 3rd — course failure; AI assistance is allowed with explicit
citation of the tool and a description of its contribution; submitting AI-generated text as your own is an
academic violation.
7.5. Design and team rules
1. A design problem is open-ended and ill-structured: there is no single answer; “best” is determined by
the client's critical requirements.
2. Define the problem in terms of needs, not solutions: a solution in the statement closes the door on
other solutions.
3. The eight steps of the design process (Kosky): define the problem → generate alternatives → evaluate
and select → detail → defend → build and test → evaluate performance → final report.
4. The two goals of a systematic approach: remove personal biases; maximum thinking and information
gathering before the final choice.
5. Design notebook: number and date the pages; do not tear pages out; do not rewrite a fair copy; use
pen; strike through, do not erase; paste in the printouts; write for another reader; record the meetings.
6. Brainstorming rules: no criticism while ideas are being offered; one person speaks; a facilitator; write
everything down; do not tie an idea to a person; afterwards — shortlist the promising ideas without
evaluating them in detail.
7. Team versus group: a shared goal and coordination; the leader delegates, communicates, keeps humor
and confidence, and sets an example.
8. Project management 3S (Dym): scope, schedule, spending; tools — Gantt (task bars over time) and
PERT (a network, the critical path).

9.3. Ten one-line answers (for quick revision)
1. An engineer = a creative person solving practical problems (ingenium).
2. Science explains, design invents the form, engineering builds what works.
3. A system = elements + processes transforming inputs into outputs, in an operating context.

7. A problem is stated as a need, not a solution (the solution-free test).
8. A variable = a number + units; performance / design / context.
9. D — a must, W — nice to have; numbers even if only rough.
10. Need → Know → How → Solve; units in brackets; significant figures only in the final answer.
